CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H
Patched

Unaffected
  • <7.2.0

Description

Before writing an entry whose path goes through a symlink, ZipArchive::extract checks the symlink's target against the destination directory. That check compares the paths as text and does not follow symlinks, and from 7.2.0 it drops the root and prefix of an absolute target before comparing. Symlinks taken from the archive were created without any check of their targets.

A crafted archive can first create a symlink that points outside the destination, then a second symlink whose target looks like a path inside the destination but goes through the first one, and then a file entry under the second symlink. The file is written outside the destination directory, for example over an existing file in the user's home directory, and extract still returns Ok(()). On Windows, a target on another drive or share whose path otherwise matches the destination passes the check directly (creating symlinks there needs Developer Mode or administrator rights). The attacker has to know or guess the absolute path of the destination directory.

This affects ZipArchive::extract and ZipArchive::extract_unwrapped_root_dir.

The fix resolves symlink targets one component at a time from the canonicalized destination, following symlinks on the way, and refuses to create a symlink, or write through one, that leads outside the destination.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0548: Vulnerability in zip
entry.summary: `ZipStreamReader` extracts entries under local-header names that can differ from the central directory
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0548

ZipStreamReader extracts entries under local-header names that can differ from the central directory
Reported
October 17, 2026
Issued
November 17, 2026
Package
zip (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • privilege-escalation
Keywords
#parser-differential #local-file-header #central-directory
Aliases
  • CVE-2026-115905
  • GHSA-m665-v7pm-7grj
References
  • https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/commit/8068ab480ccf8daa7411424e365fcdbe6d09443e
Patched
  • >=9.0.5

Description

A ZIP archive names each entry twice: in the local file header in front of the entry's data, and in the central directory at the end of the archive. ZipArchive lists and opens entries by their central-directory names. ZipStreamReader::visit and ZipStreamReader::extract, like read_zipfile_from_stream, read the local headers in order and use the local-header names without comparing them with the central directory.

An archive can therefore show one set of file names to code that inspects it with ZipArchive and write files under other names when it is extracted with ZipStreamReader. If an application checks an archive one way and extracts it the other way, an attacker can get files written or overwritten inside the destination directory that the check never saw.

The fix adds an opt-in check. ZipStreamReader::enforce_header_consistency(true) compares each local header with its central-directory entry (name, sizes, CRC-32, compression method, flags and modification time) and fails extraction on a mismatch; ZipReadOptions::enforce_header_consistency(true) and ZipArchive::validate_header_consistency() do the same for ZipArchive. The check is off by default, so upgrading alone does not change what ZipStreamReader::new(...) extracts: applications that extract untrusted archives with ZipStreamReader need to turn it on.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

Description

For WinZip AES (AE-1 and AE-2) entries, the 10-byte HMAC authentication code was read and checked only after the reader had consumed exactly the entry's declared compressed size. If the archive ended before that size was reached, the read returned end-of-stream and the truncated plaintext was accepted without the check. The authentication code of an entry with no encrypted data was never checked.

AES-CTR ciphertext can be changed bit by bit without the password, and AE-2 entries carry no CRC-32, so an attacker who can modify an archive can alter the decrypted contents of such an entry without any error being reported.

This affects reading AES-encrypted entries with a password (for example ZipArchive::by_name_decrypt) with the aes-crypto feature.

The fix returns an error when the data ends before the declared size, and checks the authentication code of empty entries.

Description

In hickory-proto 0.25.0-alpha.3 through 0.26.0-alpha.1, NSEC3 NODATA validation returned a secure result for a query at the zone apex even when no NSEC3 record in the response matched the hash of the query name, which RFC 5155 section 8.5 requires. Someone who can answer or modify DNS responses could replay any genuine signed NSEC3 record from the zone with the zone's signed SOA record and get a denial of any record type at the apex accepted as secure.

From 0.26.0-beta.1 the DNSSEC validation code lives in the hickory-net crate, where this was fixed in hickory-net 0.26.2. No hickory-proto release contains a fix. Users of DNSSEC validation in hickory-proto 0.25 or 0.26.0-alpha.1 (directly or through hickory-resolver or hickory-recursor) should move to the 0.26.2 or later releases, which validate through hickory-net.

Description

Affected versions of actix-http skip a bare line feed (LF) inside an HTTP/1.1 chunked trailer instead of rejecting the invalid line ending. Trailer lines must end with a carriage return and line feed (CRLF).

For example, after 0\r\nX\n, the parser continues reading trailer data. If a request follows on the same connection, its head can be consumed as part of the trailer, so that request is never dispatched. If no more bytes arrive, body decoding waits for more input instead of reporting an error. A remote client can trigger these effects without authentication.

Request smuggling additionally requires an HTTP intermediary that forwards the malformed body but uses a different request boundary. The tested HTTP intermediaries either rejected the input or consumed and normalized it before forwarding. Proxy access-control bypass, cache poisoning, and effects on other users were not demonstrated.

Upgrade to actix-http 3.21.1 or later. The fix rejects bare LF and invalid control bytes in trailers before consuming the following request, while preserving partial reads and valid CRLF-terminated trailers.

Patched
  • >=3.21.3

Description

Affected versions of actix-http do not track quoted strings when parsing HTTP/1.1 chunk extensions. A carriage return inside a quoted extension value is treated as the end of the chunk-size line, even if the closing quote is missing. For example, 0;x="\r\n\r\n is accepted as the end of a chunked body, and a following pipelined request is dispatched on the same connection.

A remote client can trigger this without authentication. CR and LF are invalid inside HTTP quoted strings, including after a backslash; they must be rejected rather than interpreted as framing or accepted as quoted data.

Request smuggling requires an upstream intermediary that forwards the malformed input while using a different request boundary. Dispatching two requests on the sender's own connection does not by itself demonstrate an authorization bypass or an effect on another user. Proxy bypass, cache poisoning, and cross-user response mixing were not demonstrated by the reproduction.

Upgrade to actix-http 3.21.3 or later. The fix preserves quote and escape state across reads and rejects invalid control bytes inside quoted strings and quoted pairs before consuming the following body or request bytes.

Patched

Description

Affected versions of actix-http apply the request header timeout only to the first request on an HTTP/1 connection. When data arrives for a later request, the dispatcher clears the idle keep-alive timer without starting a request header timer.

A remote client without authentication can complete one request, send one byte of a second request, and leave the connection open indefinitely without sending more data. The same problem occurs when a complete pipelined request is followed by a partial request in the same read. Repeating this can exhaust connection or file-descriptor limits and prevent new connections from being accepted. The effect depends on the server's resource limits and upstream connection controls.

Upgrade to actix-http 3.21.2 or later. The fix applies the configured request header timeout to later partial requests, including those left in the buffer after a complete pipelined request. Additional bytes do not renew the deadline. The timeout covers request headers, not upload bodies.

If an upgrade is not possible, disable HTTP keep-alive, for example with HttpServer::keep_alive(KeepAlive::Disabled) in actix-web. Connection limits can reduce resource use but do not make stalled connections expire.

RUSTSEC-2026-0557

Unsigned NSEC or NSEC3 record used in a nonexistence proof when another record at the same name is signed
Reported

Type

#dns #dnssec #nsec #nsec3
Aliases

References
  • https://github.com/hickory-dns/hickory-dns/commit/68cb330eb7e73a7db0cec9a25888db9f4bcf2086
Patched
  • >=0.26.2

Description

When DNSSEC validation collected the NSEC and NSEC3 records from a response's authority section to check a denial of existence, it kept a record if any authority record with the same owner name had validated, not only if that record itself had. A response could therefore pair a correctly signed record with a forged NSEC or NSEC3 record of the same owner name, and the forged record was used in the nonexistence proof.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can use this to get a forged NXDOMAIN or NODATA answer accepted as secure.

This affects DNSSEC validation through DnssecDnsHandle when built with dnssec-ring or dnssec-aws-lc-rs.

The fix keeps an NSEC or NSEC3 record only when its own signature validated.

RUSTSEC-2026-0556

NSEC3 NODATA at a zone apex accepted without an NSEC3 record matching the query name
Reported

Type

Keywords
#dns #dnssec #nsec3
Aliases

References
  • https://github.com/hickory-dns/hickory-dns/commit/ffdfb295d1abaad42df126c8cdd924cac74b81c0
Patched
  • >=0.26.2

Description

RFC 5155 section 8.5 says a NODATA response proven with NSEC3 needs an NSEC3 record whose hashed owner name equals the hash of the query name, and whose type bitmap has neither the query type nor CNAME.

NSEC3 NODATA validation skipped this when the query name was the zone apex (the SOA owner). If no NSEC3 record matched the query name, no closest encloser was found and no wildcard applied, it still returned a secure result.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay any genuine signed NSEC3 record from the zone together with the zone's signed SOA record, and get a NODATA answer for any record type at the apex accepted as secure. A recursor caches that denial for the negative TTL.

This affects DNSSEC validation through DnssecDnsHandle when built with dnssec-ring or dnssec-aws-lc-rs.

The fix treats such a response as bogus.

Patched

Description

When DNSSEC validation grouped a response's records into RRsets, it did not take the DNS class into account, and records of a class other than IN were left out before signatures were checked. If the IN records validated, the records of other classes (such as CH or HS) were marked secure too.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can add forged records of another class to a response and have them returned as validated. A forged DS record of another class can also get past validation, which lets any DNSKEY for the child zone be accepted and any answer from that zone be forged. How much this matters depends on how the application treats records of an unexpected class.

This affects DNSSEC validation through DnssecDnsHandle when built with dnssec-ring or dnssec-aws-lc-rs.

The fix rejects a whole response if any record in its answer, authority or additional section has a class different from the query's.

entry.summary: Long Retry token can panic or exhaust memory in a QUIC client
entry.content:

RUSTSEC-2026-0524

Long Retry token can panic or exhaust memory in a QUIC client
Reported
September 30, 2026
Issued
November 13, 2026
Package
quinn-proto (crates.io)
Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • denial-of-service
Keywords
#quic #panic #oom
Aliases
  • GHSA-wppq-2f6r-wfvm
References
  • https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/commit/3bba467893ceff64d6cda0b3a2c51a1429e10372
  • https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/commit/d45b5136ed1d5b2b04ff6456443c0662acf1d0d3
  • https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/commit/74c33ff75281d7751488e410e21e4f030782b655
  • https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/commit/a6e78d1c8bf28630f1e92fbcc38f60e0a134b01a
Patched
  • >=0.11.19
Unaffected
  • <0.11.0

Description

A client kept the token from a Retry packet without any length limit and put it into the header of every Initial packet it sent afterwards. Initial datagrams are 1200 bytes. When the token and connection IDs left no room for the minimum payload, PacketBuilder::new computed a minimum packet size larger than the maximum, which only a debug assertion checked. On the next poll_transmit, debug builds panic, and release builds try to allocate more than 10 GiB in one call. With longer tokens the allocation fails and the process aborts.

A matching Retry packet can be built from the client's first Initial alone. The attacker can therefore be the server being contacted, or anyone who sees that Initial and can answer before the server does. Every application that makes outgoing connections with quinn-proto is affected, including all quinn clients. Servers do not process Retry packets.

The fix closes the connection with PROTOCOL_VIOLATION when an Initial token leaves too little room for frames. That covers Retry tokens and cached address-validation tokens, since both come from the peer. It also reserves room for CONNECTION_CLOSE after large Initial headers. Both changes are in 0.11.19.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

entry.title: RUSTSEC-2026-0523: Vulnerability in quinn-proto
entry.summary: MAX_STREAM_DATA frame can open streams beyond the stream limit
entry.content:
History ⋅ Edit ⋅ JSON (OSV)

RUSTSEC-2026-0523

MAX_STREAM_DATA frame can open streams beyond the stream limit
Reported
September 30, 2026
Issued
November 13, 2026
Package

Type
Vulnerability
Categories
  • denial-of-service
Keywords
#quic #stream-limit #oom
Aliases
  • GHSA-53rm-773f-4q8c
References
  • https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/commit/3eb7465d9e11d7a245e99cde1a4eb872ec26d264
  • https://github.com/quinn-rs/quinn/commit/73114d8289d42bd536c790fa00a9beed05a4e5fa
Patched
  • >=0.11.19
Unaffected
  • <0.11.0

Description

When a MAX_STREAM_DATA frame named a peer-initiated bidirectional stream that was not open yet, received_max_stream_data treated the stream, and every lower-numbered stream, as opened without checking the stream ID against the limit advertised to the peer. RFC 9000 section 4.6 requires closing the connection with STREAM_LIMIT_ERROR in this case, and the STREAM and RESET_STREAM handlers already did so.

After the handshake, a peer can send one small MAX_STREAM_DATA frame naming a very large stream index, and accept then yields every stream up to that index. In quinn, a loop that keeps calling accept_bi can be handed more than 2^40 streams. Depending on the runtime, the endpoint runs out of memory, stops accepting new connections, or keeps busy indefinitely, even after the peer has gone away. Clients and servers that accept peer-initiated bidirectional streams are affected. Unidirectional streams are not.

The fix validates the stream ID in received_max_stream_data and adds a defensive check where streams are opened implicitly. It is in 0.11.19.

Advisory available under CC0-1.0 license.

References

  • https://github.com/libp2p/rust-libp2p/pull/6525
Patched
  • >=0.13.1

Description

After the QUIC handshake finished, the peer's libp2p TLS certificate was parsed a second time to get its peer ID, and the result was unwrapped with expect, on the assumption that it could not fail because the certificate had already been validated. Parsing checks the certificate's validity period again against the current time. A remote peer can present a certificate that is about to expire and delay the end of the handshake until it has expired, so the second parse fails and the process panics. No authentication is needed; any application with a reachable QUIC listener is affected.

The fix returns a connection error instead of panicking when the peer identity or certificate cannot be read after the handshake. It is in 0.13.1, and was backported to the main branch in libp2p/rust-libp2p#6525 for 0.14.0.

Description

The MathML text integration points (mi, mo, mn, ms, mtext) and SVG foreignObject can be made to contain a tag in the other one's namespace (a MathML integration point with a child in the SVG namespace, or vice versa) without the root tag that switches out of the HTML namespace. If the attacker can construct input that parses differently in as HTML than as foreign XML, they can inject arbitrary JavaScript code into the user's browser.

For example:

  • The user writes <math><mi><svg><gadget></svg></mi></math>.
  • The application enables math, mi, and the gadget, but not svg.
  • Ammonia filters the input to <math><mi><gadget></mi></math>.
  • Because svg is now gone, the gadget switches from being parsed as SVG to being parsed as HTML.
  • The gadget is written in such a way that it exploits the parsing differences between HTML and MathML.

As far as we know, the gadget can only be written using a tag that is parsed as raw text in HTML. These elements are:

  • title
  • textarea
  • xmp
  • iframe
  • noembed
  • noframes
  • plaintext
  • noscript
  • style
  • script

Applications that do not explicitly allow any of these tags should not be affected, since none are allowed by default.

This vulnerability was reported by Roger Meyer.

Description

Some targets read one datagram per recvmsg call instead of using recvmmsg: Apple platforms without the fast-apple-datapath feature, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Solaris and illumos, and from 0.6 also DragonFly BSD, Redox and GNU/Hurd. On these targets the receive loop set up its msghdr only once and looked at the MSG_TRUNC flag before checking whether recvmsg had failed. After a datagram larger than the receive buffer was dropped, a following EAGAIN still saw the old truncation flag. The loop then kept issuing non-blocking receives instead of returning WouldBlock.

When the receive buffer is smaller than a datagram that arrives, a remote sender can keep the task that drives the socket busy, before any QUIC packet authentication. The loop ends only when a later datagram fits in the buffer. Whether an application is exposed therefore depends on the receive buffer size it uses. Linux, Android, FreeBSD and Windows use other receive paths and are not affected.

The fix rebuilds the header before every recvmsg call and returns receive errors before checking the truncation flag. It is in 0.5.16 and 0.6.3.

Unaffected

Description

When an upstream answer had the TC (truncated) bit set, the resolver's name server pool disabled UDP and sent the query again. It did this for every truncated answer, including answers that already came over TCP, and it kept no count of retries.

From 0.26.2 a truncated answer received after UDP has already been disabled ends the lookup with NetError::Truncated instead of retrying again.

Unaffected

Description

When a referral listed name servers outside the delegated zone and gave no glue addresses, the recursor looked up A and AAAA records for every listed name server, recursing into each one. Only the chain-depth limits applied. There was no cap on how many name servers it chased per referral or on the total upstream work per client query.

Someone who controls a zone can return referrals that list many glueless name servers in a victim's domain, and nest them, so that each client query makes the recursor send a large number of queries to the victim's servers (the NXNSAttack pattern). The same can exhaust the recursor's own resources.

This affects the recursive resolver, which is in hickory-resolver behind the opt-in recursor feature from 0.26.0-beta.1. Earlier releases shipped it as the separate hickory-recursor crate.

From 0.26.2 the recursor follows at most 5 glueless name servers per delegation and sends at most 200 upstream queries per client request.

Description

When an NSEC record's next domain name is below the queried name, the queried name exists as an empty non-terminal (RFC 8020 section 3.1). The NSEC validator did not check for this case and accepted an NXDOMAIN response backed by such a record as secure.

The fix rejects NXDOMAIN as bogus, and validates NODATA as secure, when the covering NSEC record's next domain name is below the queried name and is not the zone apex. It is in 0.26.2.

Description

The DNSSEC validation cache used a 64-bit hash of the query as its key, and two keys with the same hash counted as equal. The Hash implementation of Name hashed the bytes of the labels but not where one label ends and the next begins, so names that differ only in the placement of dots (such as ab.c. and a.bc.) hashed to the same value.

An attacker who controls an unsigned delegation whose name collides in this way with a name in a signed zone can first get an Insecure result cached for their own name. A forged response for the signed name is then served from that cache entry without signature checks and returned with the AD bit clear, where validation should have failed.

This affects DNSSEC validation through DnssecDnsHandle when built with dnssec-ring or dnssec-aws-lc-rs.

The fix stores the query in the cache key and compares it on lookup. The Hash implementations of Label, Name and LowerName in hickory-proto were also changed to include label boundaries. Both are in 0.26.2.

Description

cap-primitives resolves a path inside a sandboxed directory one component at a time and opens the last component with O_NOFOLLOW, so that a symlink there cannot lead out of the directory. When the path ended in /, the resolver added the slash back to the last component before opening it. With a trailing slash the operating system no longer treats that component as the last one, so O_NOFOLLOW does not apply, the symlink is followed, and the resulting file descriptor was returned without further checks.

A symlink inside the sandbox that points outside it, such as escape -> ../outside or a link to /, can therefore be opened as escape/. If the symlink's own target ends in /, the caller's path does not need a trailing slash at all, so removing trailing slashes from untrusted input is not a workaround. The maintainers' advisory reports reads and writes outside the sandbox through open, open_dir, read_dir and canonicalize, and directory creation, removal and renames outside it through create_dir, remove_dir and rename.

This resolver is used on Windows and macOS, on FreeBSD when O_RESOLVE_BENEATH is not available, and on Linux when openat2 is not available (kernels before 5.6, or a seccomp policy that rejects it). cap-std and other crates built on cap-primitives are affected through it. Wasmtime's WASI filesystem support was affected as well; that is covered by RUSTSEC-2026-0269.

The fix stops re-adding the trailing slash and is in 3.4.6 and 4.0.3.

Description

tdx_guest::tdcall::invalidate_l2_cached_ept() takes a bitmap that selects the L2 VMs whose cached EPT translations should be invalidated. Bits 1 through 3 select L2 VMs 1 through 3, and all other bits are reserved. The input check was inverted:

    return Err(TdCallError::TdxOperandInvalid);

Description

The extended-attribute functions in rustix::fs (getxattr, lgetxattr, fgetxattr, listxattr, llistxattr and flistxattr) write into a Buffer and then mark as many bytes initialized as the system call reported. When the buffer has zero length, the operating system treats the call as a size query: it writes nothing and returns the size of the attribute value or of the name list. rustix still marked that many bytes as initialized.

Passing a Vec whose length equals its capacity through spare_capacity gives such a zero-length buffer, and rustix then set the vector's length past its capacity over memory that was never written. This is undefined behavior reachable from safe code. With an empty &mut [MaybeUninit<u8>] the call panics instead.

From 1.1.6 these functions return an empty result for a zero-length buffer, and new getxattr_query, lgetxattr_query, fgetxattr_query, listxattr_query, llistxattr_query and flistxattr_query functions return the size. The 0.38 series did not have the Buffer API and is not affected.
